en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who bore the burden of the tradition of the illustrious Guru Prabhākara.
Adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and the gloss on difficult passages (*viṣamasthala-ṭippaṇī*), here begins the 107th chapter, named *Pramāṇapārāyaṇa*.
The Sixth Chapter.
The First Section on Direct Perception: A Declaration of the Subject Matter of the Chapter.
Since disputants have extensively propagated various disagreements regarding its essential nature, number, object, and result, [this chapter is composed].
Therefore, for the sake of achieving an awakening to that [reality], we begin this thorough study of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (1)
Furthermore, what is this so-called "valid cognition" (pramāṇa)? It cannot be non-discrepant cognition (*avisaṃvādi-jñāna*),
because that would entail the undesirable consequence that even memory (*smṛti*) would be valid cognition.

Furthermore, if memory— being conceptual in nature— does not grasp the ultimately real particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), but instead delineates a non-substantial aspect that exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*), then like the cognition of a double moon and so forth, it would not be non-contradictory; thus, even in this case, inference would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it too is conceptual in nature.
In that case, inference, although having a conceptual form and lacking a real entity as its object, is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) as if it had a real entity as its object;
thus, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it does not contradict the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is the real entity being so determined.
Memory would likewise be [a valid means of knowledge].
For that [conceptual cognition] also arises as one that determines only its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, how could an inference be non-contradictory if it determines an object that is not a real entity to be a real entity, like the [erroneous] determination of mother-of-pearl as silver?
Moreover, if inference, being conceptual in nature, does not grasp the specific characteristic, [it cannot be non-contradictory].
How, then, can there even be a determination?
For there is no such thing as determination other than grasping;
for how could that aspect which is not grasped be determined at all?
And this which is stated—that "recollection, like inference, does not take an external object as its domain"—is contradicted by common experience;
for even though those two are conceptual in nature, they are perceived to grasp objects that have been directly perceived.
Now, it might be argued: "We do not assert that [recollection] is non-contradictory in the sense of grasping an object exactly as it exists..."
However, it is that which leads to the attainment of a thing capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-samartha*);
for if a thing is shown exactly as it is, then even one who acts upon it obtains precisely such a thing.
At that time, a cognition that is non-discrepant with that [object] is called a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And so it has been said: “A valid means of knowledge is non-discrepant cognition; non-discrepancy is the stability of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsthiti*)... [Pramāṇavārttika, Chapter 1, Verse 3]. Likewise: “For one who acts after having determined an object by means of these two [types of cognition] is not deceived regarding purposeful action.”
And even so, it would follow that memory possesses validity.
Now, if it is thought that one who acts toward an object after having remembered it does not necessarily obtain that object—
Even so, inference whose object is a real thing would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*),
for there is no attainment of the object demonstrated by it.
Now, even if there is no attainment of the real entity cognized through inference, [the objection remains].

Nevertheless, because it arises from a mark (liṅga) that is invariably concomitant with that [object], it certainly possesses the capacity for attainment; and by that much alone, its status as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is established.
Even so, memory would result in being a valid means of knowledge.
For even memory, like inference, is connected to the object only through a causal chain:
just as from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire comes the specific characteristic of smoke,
and from that comes the perception of smoke.

From that [perception] arises the conceptualization of smoke, and from that, inference; thus, because it is indirectly connected with the object through this succession, inference is non-discrepant with the object and capable of attaining the object. Likewise, memory is also [non-discrepant], for experience arises from the object.

From that [cognition] comes the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and from the mental impression comes memory; thus, being strictly bound to the object, it would become a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its fitness to reach that object.
If one should think: "Even though there is fitness for reaching the object, as for the specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is to be reached by that memory,"
Memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it brings about [an object] that has already been reached through prior experience;
inference, however, is a means of valid cognition because it brings about the attainment of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) not yet attained.
Even so, the mere fact of bringing about the attainment of an entity capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-samartha*) is not the definition of a means of valid cognition.
However, the qualification must be adopted:
"Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory knowledge that brings about what has not yet been attained.
Now, it might be argued that for one who has already attained [an object], no other [cognition] possesses the quality of being a bringer-about (*prāpaka*).
That is incorrect;
for being "that which leads to attainment" consists in being connected with the object,
and that is not impossible even for another cognition.
If it were argued that validity does not consist merely in being a means of attainment,
but also in being a motivator; then, that which both brings about attainment and motivates action—
And as for the claim that "only that [first cognition] is a means of valid cognition," this too is of no consequence;
for even another subsequent cognition can indeed possess the capacity to induce action (*pravartakatā*).

The quality of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*) consists precisely in the capacity to present an object suitable for engagement; and this quality belongs to recollection just as it does to inference whose object is a real entity (*bhūtārtha*).
Furthermore, if [instigating power] were to enter into the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then non-conceptual cognitions (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) would be rendered invalid.
Because [perception] itself lacks the capacity to initiate practical activity (*vyavahāra*),
it is only the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arising from it that would be considered valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being the means of attainment and the instigators of action.

Furthermore, in the case of continuous streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*), subsequent cognitions would lack the status of valid cognition because their objects are already contained within the object of the preceding cognition.
Now, it might be argued:
"It is indeed accepted that those [cognitions] are not valid means of knowledge.
That is incorrect.
In the world, because their status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is no different from that of the former,
even investigators must follow worldly standards of validity.
Now, if it is argued that because the moments of objects (*arthakṣaṇa*) are distinct, all [cognitions] possess the quality of making one attain what has not yet been attained;
That is incorrect;

since the distinction between moments is not perceived, it is not appropriate for validity to depend upon that. Furthermore, momentariness has already been refuted in the *Mīmāṃsājīvarakṣā*, so let us refrain from further elaboration.

A refutation of the definition of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as accepted by the Bhāṭṭas: Nor is the definition of valid cognition as "that which apprehends an object not already apprehended and is non-contradictory" tenable;
for this would exclude the validity of subsequent cognitions in a continuous stream (dhārāvāhika-jñāna), since they have as their object an entity already perceived in the preceding moment.
Nor can validity be established by the determination of a difference in time,
because even if such a difference in time exists, it is not perceived due to its extreme subtlety.
Furthermore, what is there to be removed by the cognition "I see"?

If it is argued that this is "doubtful cognition" (*saṃśayajñāna*), what then is this doubt? It is a cognition whose object is an indefinite particularity regarding a thing whose particularity has not been determined; [it arises] from the perception of a common property, or from the apprehension of multiple properties in one thing, or from the conflicting assertions of disputants regarding particulars that are being considered, all of which occur with respect to a thing whose specific nature remains undetermined.

The logicians maintain that cognition is doubt, as for example when, regarding an object whose specific features are concealed by deep darkness, one perceives only its verticality and wonders, "Is this a post or a person?
Likewise: "Wind is perceptible because it possesses touch, like the earth."
Likewise: "Air is imperceptible because it lacks color, like space.
Because of the dispute among proponents—some saying that sound is eternal and others saying it is non-eternal—a seeker of truth develops doubt regarding its true nature.
That is incorrect;
for when two properties are being doubted,
this single cognition does not arise with respect to both of them.
However, these two cognitions are memories of qualifiers;

and since there is no certainty regarding even one of those two qualifiers with respect to that subject (*dharmin*), the cognizer, being unable to engage in a definitive practical activity (*vyavahāra*), becomes as if in doubt— thus, there occurs a "doubtful" practical activity.

Furthermore, since the validity of recollection has already been refuted on the grounds that it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitā*), what is the purpose of including the term "perception" (*dṛk*)?
Moreover, the inclusion of the term "non-discrepant" (*avisamvādi*) is also non-distinctive, because all cognitions do not deviate from their objects.
[Objection: But is there not the cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl?
Furthermore, it is observed that the cognition of a reflection is erroneous;
this is not so.
If the cognition of silver were not to have silver as its object, [it would be erroneous].
Therefore, it deviates from the object.
But if its object is silver, what deviation is there?
Is it not the case that this cognition does not have silver as its object?
But it concerns only the mother-of-pearl.
It is said:
what is the meaning of "concerning the mother-of-pearl"?
Does it take as its object that very individual instance of mother-of-pearl, or does it take "mother-of-pearl-ness" itself?
First of all, that individual instance of mother-of-pearl cannot be made an object by this [cognition].
This is because there is a difference between the form and that which possesses the form.
Furthermore, even a correct manifestation of silver does not fail to become an object of the cognition "silver-ness," so how much less so the manifestation of mother-of-pearl?
Furthermore, it is not tenable that "shell-ness" (śuktikatva) is the object while remaining unmanifest.
If it were argued that being an object consists in the attainment of fitness for practical transaction (vyavahāra-yogyatā), even so,
shell-ness would still not be an object at all.
For that [silver] does not attain the state of being fit for conventional linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
Being manifest is itself the nature of being an object (*viṣayatva*);
therefore, it is precisely the "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) that is the object.
And since that [object] is not possible in what stands before one, this [cognition] is merely a memory having that as its object; how, then, could it be erroneous?
As for the cognition of a reflection, it has the face and so forth as its object, appearing as the face and so forth.

For when the ray of the eye falls upon a bright surface such as a mirror, it is struck back and turned around; having come into contact with the face and so forth, it perceives that very face and so forth.
But even so, the reversal of left and right,
as well as the appearance of differences in location and the smallness or greatness of dimensions, would remain without a basis.
To this, it is replied:

The location of the face and so forth is not perceived, while the mirror and other such objects are indeed perceived; thus, the face and other features appear as if they were located in that [mirror's] place.

Since the visual ray is joined with the face and so forth by means of its being directed toward it, it perceives them exactly in that way; therefore, the reversal of left and right is entirely logical.

As for smallness and largeness, due to the defect consisting in the smallness or largeness of the mirror and other objects—which causes the obstruction of the visual rays—the actual dimensions of the face and so forth are not grasped, and instead, the dimensions of the mirror and other objects are grasped; consequently, these [dimensions] appear to belong to the face and other features.
Therefore, there is no deviation [from the definition].

This and other such points have been established more skillfully in the *Nayavīthī*; thus, following this very direction, one must avoid deviation in all cases. Consequently, even this is not a valid definition of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
[Now follows] the definition of a means of knowledge as accepted by the Prābhākara school.
Now he states his own intended definition of perception and shows that it does not entail the status of memory as a valid means of knowledge: "It is other than memory. Now, what is memory?
"Memory, moreover, is said to be a cognition produced solely from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous cognition."
And thus, serial cognitions (dhārāvāhika-jñāna) do not possess the nature of memory,
because they arise from the contact of the sense organ with its object, just like [the first cognition] before; furthermore,
due to the inclusion of the word "only" (mātra), recognition (pratyabhijñāna) does not have the nature of memory.
Now, why is memory not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
To this he says: "Memory is not a means of valid cognition because it depends upon a prior apprehension.
For memory, arising as the thought "that," conforms to a previous cognition and does not determine its object independently; therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition.
In that case, the loss of memory would be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). No;
for that too is entirely dependent upon a prior cognition, since its production depends solely upon the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) generated by it.

To the objection—“In the case of continuous cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*), how can the subsequent cognitions be valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when they are indistinguishable from one another due to the loss of memory?”—the author says: “But the successive cognitions in a stream are independent of one another.

For while the causal complex of the preceding cognition is still functioning, the subsequent ones also arise; thus, neither in terms of their production nor in terms of their apprehension do the successive cognitions in a stream differ from each other. Therefore, it is logical that all of them possess the status of being valid means of knowledge.
If mere experience were the means of valid cognition, then even that erroneous cognition which thinks "this is silver" would be a means of valid cognition.
To this it is replied:
"This is silver"—this is not a single cognition;
rather, these are two cognitions, consisting of perception and recollection.
In that case, the recollection "this is silver" does not entail the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) because it lacks the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*).
The cognition "this" (*idam*), being of the nature of direct experience, is indeed accepted as a valid means of knowledge.
It is the cognition of silver alone that possesses the character of an error (*bhrānti*).
Because it initiates the process of apprehension and linguistic usage, it is non-contradictory in practical discourse (*vyavahāra*).

Furthermore, even those who maintain that this single cognition is false must admit that falsity depends upon a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*); they are thus unable to claim that the "this" (*idam*) component itself is false.
In that regard, because there is an absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*),
and because the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*) persists even during the state of a subverting cognition,
it is entirely logical that even a single cognition— though based on a distinction determined by its object— can be both valid (*pramāṇa*) and invalid (*apramāṇa*).
In that case, it would follow that the cognition of a yellow conch and so forth is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For in that instance, both the yellowness and the true nature of the conch are indeed experienced.
Indeed, it has been demonstrated with great precision in the *Nayavīthī* that the yellowness residing in the bile-substance located in the eye is also experienced.
Regarding the true nature of the conch shell, the experience is indeed non-contradictory;
this is not a fault.
For who would say that the cognition of a yellow conch shell is invalid?
For that alone is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its object corresponds to reality;
whereas these two cognitions possess a form common to a single underlying cognition.

In that regard, because it apprehends a form common to a single cognition and thereby initiates a conventional usage similar to that single cognition, it is called "erroneous" even though it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since it brings about non-correspondence during the state of conventional usage;
however, where there is no non-correspondence in conventional usage, it is not designated as erroneous.
As in the cognition of hot water;
even there, the heat residing in the water is not experienced, but rather that which resides in the particles of fire alone.
Furthermore, it is not accepted that the heat residing in water is produced through conjunction with fire;
for a quality born of maturation (*pākaja*) ceases only through another act of maturation.
However, the heat residing in water—which does not depend on maturation—ceases solely through the cessation of the conjunction with fire.

For in that case, the particles of heat are mobile; when they have moved elsewhere and the flow of other heat-particles has ceased, it is logical that the cognition of heat—which is not produced by cooking (*apākaja*)—does not depend on a subsequent act of cooking.
Thus, the cognition of warm water is not equivalent to the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and the like.
Therefore, it is faultless to maintain that the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and the like is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even though it is erroneous (*bhrānta*).

However, for one who maintains the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) and asserts that the cognition of "hot water" is both invalid and erroneous, there is a contradiction with the consensus of all the world.
[This concludes] the determination of the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the question of how many kinds of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there are, he says: “In that regard, the means of knowledge is fivefold.
By this, numbers such as one and so forth, as well as numbers such as six and so forth, are excluded.

What, then, are those means of knowledge? To this he says: "The treatise (śāstra), as well as comparison (upamāna) and presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)—this is the opinion of the Guru. This is a restatement of the definition of perception (pratyakṣa) as stated by Gautama. What, then, is the definition of perception?
Some say: "Perception is knowledge produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature.
That knowledge which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with an object is perception.

In that regard, that contact is divided into six types: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), [conjunction-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*)], [inherence-in-conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*)], [inherence (*samavāya*)], [inherence-in-inherent (*samavetasamavāya*)], and [non-existence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā*)].
Inherence in that which is conjoined, inherence in that which is inherent in what is conjoined, and inherence.
Inherence in that which is inherent (samavetasamavāya) and the state of being a qualifier of the conjoined (saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā).
Among these, through conjunction, there is the perception by means of sight and touch of substances belonging to earth, water, fire, and air.
The eye reaches its object, because it is an external sense organ, like the sense organ of touch.
It is composed of light, because it is the cause of the perception of color, like a lamp.
Its rays, as they spread forth, come into contact with the substance.
And because they have broad tips (*pṛthvagrā*), they reach even large objects.
[Objection: But if this were so, there would be no perception of an interval when an object is at a distance;
for if there is contact (*prāpti*), distance is impossible, since [the sense organ] functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*), just like the sense of touch (*sparśana*).

Furthermore, since conjunction is the basis for movement, and since those possessing movement travel by degrees from near to far, it would be impossible to perceive objects that are reached simultaneously, even if they are at vastly different distances.
It is replied: First, the perception of intervals is indeed possible in relation to the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*).
Regarding simultaneous cognition, however, some describe the resolution as follows:
"Having reached all objects simultaneously, those visual rays merge with the external light that has presented itself, and thus they become the cause for simultaneous perception.
Others refute this, saying: "If such reaching [of the object] is admitted, then the perception of objects that are extremely distant or obstructed would be unavoidable.
Still others say: "Because those rays are so swift, the difference in time is not perceived, leading to the misconception of simultaneity."
Others do not agree with that. [They argue:
"Let it be granted that in the case of extremely proximate objects, a difference in the time of arrival might not be perceived—like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals;

however, the constant non-perception of a difference in time regarding objects situated on the earth at a distance of many thousands of *yojanas*, as well as in the case of the polar star (*dhruva*), does not satisfy the intellect."
125. We reply: there is no fault, because it depends upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

Even when the external light has become unified with the rays of the eye, only that portion of it which is appropriated as a cause of perception by virtue of the unseen force is capable of producing perception.
"Not all [is perceived]," meaning that there is no simultaneous perception of everything, and there is the established proof of the earth, the pole star, and so forth.
But if the ocular light functions by reaching its object, how is there perception of things obstructed by glass, clouds, veils, or cataracts?
Because the rays of the eyes are unimpeded by them.
Furthermore, for those who assert that the eye acts without reaching its object (*aprāpyakārin*), the perception of objects that are obstructed or distant would be unavoidable;
for just as in close proximity, even objects that are extremely subtle would be perceived clearly despite their distance.

However, when reaching the sense organs for apprehension, because the constituent parts of light are not abundant, it is logical that those at a great distance are seen indistinctly, while those that are extremely minute are not seen at all.
Now, why is it that atoms such as earthy ones, as well as space, time, direction, and the self, are not perceived by direct perception?

It is said: magnitude (*mahattva*), the state of being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*), and a specific kind of color (*rūpaviśeṣa*) are the causes of perception, as if they were present [in the object].
This is because a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) lacks magnitude, while space (*ākāśa*) and the like lack color and are not substances composed of other substances; thus it should be understood.
In this regard, the following should be understood: three kinds of substances are perceived through conjunction by means of both sight and touch;
and through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), there is the perception of their qualities such as color and so forth, as well as of their motions;

and through inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), there is the perception of the universals of quality-ness (*guṇatva*), motion-ness (*karmatva*), color-ness (*rūpatva*), and so on.
The apprehension of sound occurs through inherence;
the auditory organ is simply the space delimited by the ear-cavity,
and sound is its quality— this has been explained more precisely in the *Tattvāloka*.

From inherence-in-the-inherent (samavetasamavāya), there is the cognition of "sound-ness" (śabdatva). The apprehension of absence occurs through its being a qualifier of that which is conjoined (saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā),
as in the case of "the branch is without fruit."
Refutation of the Naiyāyika Position: 128.

That is incorrect—129. If only largeness (*mahattva*), being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*), and possession of color-form (*rūpavattva*) were the causes of perception, then air would be imperceptible.
Nor should it be said that this is indeed accepted,
because it is perceived through touch;
for by means of that [touch], one perceives only the tactile sensation.
If it is argued that air is not a substance, [we reply] no;
for a substance is recognized as such when cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold tactile sensations are perceived.

For when the heat belonging to fire, the coldness belonging to water, and the neither-hot-nor-cold nature of air are apprehended through touch while the wind is blowing, [the substance air is thereby established].
At that time, the substance is recognized as "this is that very same thing";
therefore, it is not a cognition of mere touch.
Consequently, one must conclude that possession of touch, just like possession of color, is a cause for perception.
Furthermore, that which was stated— that actions are perceptible because they are inherent in what is conjoined [with the senses]—
is also incorrect;
for action is to be inferred from its effects, characterized by conjunction and disjunction.
This has been elaborated upon in the two *Pañcikās*,
and we shall also discuss it here in the chapter on inference (*anumāna*).

Furthermore, as for the desired apprehension of qualities such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) through the relation of inherence in that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*), [it is explained as follows].
That too is untenable precisely because those [entities] do not exist;
likewise, the apprehension of "sound-ness" (śabdatva) through inherence-in-the-inherent (samavetasamavāya) is similarly impossible.
Furthermore, why is another type of contact (sannikarṣa), namely "qualification by inherence" (samavāyaviśeṣaṇatā), not accepted?

Just as, for the sake of cognizing the mutual non-existence between a cow and a horse, another type of contact called "qualification of the conjoined" (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā*) is resorted to, so too, for the comprehension of the mutual non-existence between the phonemes *ka* and *kha*, it is appropriate to accept another type of contact characterized as "qualification of the inherent" (*samavetaviśeṣaṇatā*).
Therefore, there are only three types of contact that serve as the cause of perception: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), [inherence (*samavāya*), and qualification of the inherent (*samavetaviśeṣaṇatā*)].
[The types of contact are] conjunctional inherence and inherence.
For what purpose is the term "indescribable" [used]?
This is for the purpose of refuting the suspicion that [perception] produced by the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects might be verbal in nature.
For when one knows "this is color" or knows "this is taste," there arises in someone the suspicion that it is verbal in nature because of the possibility of association with words;
therefore, it is stated that [perception] is "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) in order to refute that.
For there is no operation of the word in a cognition produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object,
from which [operation] its status as verbal knowledge (*śābdatā*) might arise;
rather, it is the definition of perception that must be stated.
That form by which a thing is distinguished from both its own class and other classes is precisely its definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
In this regard, the distinction of [perception] from verbal cognition is already established by the very fact that it arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object.

It is appropriate to refute the suspicion that perception—which is accompanied by the internal discourse of words—might be verbal cognition during the section examining verbal cognition (the *Śābdaparīkṣā*), just as one might suspect every instance of verbal cognition to be inference.
Furthermore, it has been stated that the term "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicāri*), which was mentioned for the purpose of excluding error,
is not a distinguishing feature because all cognitions are non-erroneous.
Likewise, the quality of being "determinate in nature" (*vyavasāyātmakatā*) need not be stated for the purpose of eliminating doubt.

For the two types of recollective cognition, "Is it a post? or "Is it a person?", are not produced by the contact of the sense organ with an object; thus, there is no possibility of their being classified as perception.
Furthermore, the exclusion of doubt is already established by the very term "non-erroneous" (avyabhicārin).
For that [inference] as well, there is deviation from the object as it is being cognized.
Furthermore, non-deviation and the nature of determinate cognition (*vyavasāyātmakatā*) are not the definition of perception, but rather the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having thus formulated the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one must state the specific, individual definition for perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which is capable of distinguishing it from both similar and dissimilar classes—as follows: "Perception is that which arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object.
Even regarding this definition, the resulting cognition of inference and so forth [must be excluded] from its own self...
Furthermore, it would not be perceptual with respect to the cognizer (pramātṛ), because it is not produced by the sense organs.
This is a restatement of Dharmakīrti’s definition of perception.
Others, however, say: "Perception is that which is free from conceptual construction (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta)."
Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is the association with universals (*jāti*) and so forth;
that cognition which is devoid of such construction is perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It is stated that [perception] must be "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) so that the cognition of hair-nets and the like by those suffering from ophthalmia, which is of such a nature, might not be wrongly classified as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, there is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors,
and mental [perception] (*mānasa*).
And there is the knowledge of the yogi.
That which arises from the contact of the sense faculties with their objects is sensory cognition; it is fivefold, pertaining to the five [objects] beginning with form.
The self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of all cognitions is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, pleasure and the like do not differ from that cognition because they share the same causes as the cognition; thus, they too are indeed self-cognized.
Mental cognition (*mānasa*), however, is produced by sensory cognition acting in conjunction with the moment immediately following its own object-moment.
And the object to be grasped by that sensory cognition is its immediately preceding moment.
Now, since the objective moment that produces [the cognition] has already passed at the time when the produced cognition exists, how can the object be said to be directly perceived?
It is replied: this alone is the nature of being an object for things—that they produce [the cognition] and impart their own form [to it].
Perceptual cognition has the form of the object;
otherwise, how could a formless consciousness establish the distinction between the cognition of color-form and so forth?
For this very reason, conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because that alone is the cause for the determination [of the object],
it is consciousness that connects with the similarity of form (*sārūpya*) to the object, and not the sense faculty and so forth; therefore, the latter is not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But surely, since a single form is perceived and that form resides only within the cognition itself, how can there be direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) of the object?
It is replied: there is no fault, because whatever object causes the form of the cognition to conform to its own presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is what is directly perceived.
Furthermore, one must accept that cognition possesses a form (*sākāratā*).
Otherwise, in cases such as dreams where no external object exists, what would it be whose form is manifested?
Moreover, how could a form that is external to cognition—which is itself of the nature of luminosity—be manifested?
Because it is impossible for an insentient thing to possess luminosity;
furthermore, the simultaneous apprehension of the object and its cognition is constant.

Since this [simultaneity] is pervaded by non-difference (as difference is pervaded by non-constancy), its presence—through the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader—is excluded from difference; thus, abiding in non-difference, it leads to the inference of non-difference.
However, the appearance of duality should be understood as being based on beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), like the perception of two moons;
whereas the knowledge of the yogi arises from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of the true object.

When one cultivates an object established by valid cognition even if it is imperceptible, at the highest degree of that cultivation, there arises a cognition in which the object appears as if it were directly perceived.
That is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) due to the clarity of its manifestation.
For a cognition permeated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) cannot possess the quality of manifesting an object with clarity.
The refutation of that [position] is as follows:

because sense-cognitions (*indriya-jñāna*) that arise through the association with universals (*jāti*) and so forth—which are conceptual (*savikalpaka*)—are deprived of the status of perception (*pratyakṣatā*).
Now, it might be argued: "Since universals and qualities are not perceived as distinct from the substance, there is no difference [between them] at all."
Therefore, the claim that the cognition which arises by joining those two [entities]— which do not actually exist— is a conceptual construction of genus and quality and thus not perception,
is also incorrect.
This is because it is unproven that there is no apprehension of distinctness, since one perceives another substance as distinct from each individual substance.

This was established in the *Jātinirṇaya* [section], because even when a single substance is distinguished from other substances, a difference is perceived between the genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*), which both persist [in that substance]. Furthermore,
the postulation of action (*karma*) is indeed accepted as not being perceptible, since action is an object of inference.
The conceptualization of a substance, such as "horned" or "staff-bearer," does not transcend the status of perception;
likewise, the conceptualization of a name, such as "this is Devadatta," is also perceptual.
Because it conforms to the operation of the sense faculties, although the name consisting of phonemes is present there as an object of memory,
and the relationship of signifier and signified with it is likewise merely superimposed upon memory,
nevertheless, the cognizer does not relinquish its status as direct perception.
For neither the designation nor its connection with it appeared at that time as a qualifier within a single cognition;
rather, both of these are merely superimposed by memory.
For when the named object (*saṃjñin*) is being perceived, those two previously experienced [qualities] ascend to memory.

Therefore it has been said: "Even though the name (*saṃjñā*) is being remembered, it does not subvert the perceptual nature [of the object]. For that [name] stands apart from the named object; it is not capable of obscuring its form."
Thus, those who claim that knowledge arising through the association with a name is not perception are also refuted by this very same line of reasoning;
for the association with a name is impossible in the case of sensory cognition.
Moreover, for one who maintains that universals and qualities are not perceptible, nothing at all could be accounted as perception.
For there is no cognition of a material object that is devoid of form;
and both genus and quality reside in the form of material objects.
Indeed, every cognition arises in this manner: "It is thus."
Furthermore, the meaning of the word "evam" (thus) is "manner" (*prakāra*).

Since genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) constitute the manner of objects, all sensory cognition arises precisely by being conjoined with these two; therefore, the locus for conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is devoid of an external object.

Even the term "unmistaken" (*abhrānta*) is entirely devoid of objective referent for the Buddhists, because all cognitions appear in a gross form and are associated with the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject.
Furthermore, as for that which is called mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), we do not consider it to be anything distinct from a continuous stream of consciousness (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*).
This might be the [opponent's] thought:
159. "Sensory cognition occurs when the operation of the sense-faculties has not ceased, whereas mental cognition arises in the subsequent moment when they have ceased.

This is incorrect; for even when the operation of the sense-faculties has ceased, the result—namely, the perception of an object as if it were present before the eyes—is possible, and thus [the claim that mental cognition arises only upon their cessation] is unproven.
As for the claim that mental cognition has past objects as its domain,
that too is incorrect,
because what is perceived is the aspect of the present.
Moreover, this aspect does not belong to consciousness alone; for it appears as distinct from consciousness because it is an object of cognition,
whereas consciousness [appears] as consciousness itself.
Furthermore, since the object of cognition appears as something to be cognized,
it is not tenable that the two possess the nature of one another;
and as for what was said— that the appearance of difference is an illusion.
That too is untenable due to the absence of a cause;
nor is the very determination of the cognition of an object the cause of differentiation,
because even cognitions that are formless manifest as being connected to specific objects by their very nature.
Furthermore, that which was stated as the reason for establishing the conformity of cognition with its object is unproven,
because cognitions appear as gross [objects].
And because the object possesses a corresponding form.

Furthermore, if that similarity were defined by the characteristics of being produced from it and being cognized, then the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), which possesses an identical form, would also be cognizable.
It has been established in the *Nayavīthī* that even in dreams and similar states, the form of an external object manifests in memory; furthermore,
the argument stated— that there can be no manifestation for that which is insentient because it lacks consciousness—
is also untenable.
The connection with manifestation is possible only for that which is insentient;
however, its identity with that [manifestation] is certainly not admitted.
Furthermore, if manifestation belongs only to that which is not distinct from cognition, [then...]

In that case, how can there be a manifestation of the distinction between the grasped, the grasper, and cognition? For that [distinction], being unreal, does not enter into the very nature of knowledge. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the form and the cognition are non-different because they are necessarily perceived together—[that too is untenable].
That too is without substance;
for even if there is a difference in cognition, the restriction of the object is established. For it is precisely that very cognition [which determines it].
Since that very [cognition] is the apprehension of that object, how could it manifest without it?
And as for the self-cognition (svasaṃvedana) said to be the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of all cognitions—
that indeed we accept.
That which is intended as self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) on the grounds that pleasure and the like are non-different because they share the same cause—
that is untenable,
because the non-difference of their causes is unestablished.
Because an object is the cause of cognition,
and because cognition is the basis for pleasure and so forth;
for even when an object is not present, pleasure and so forth arise from mere cognition, as in dreams and the like.
Furthermore, that which is considered the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a yogi is also incorrect; for direct perception is indeed a specific type of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, it is not possible for the yogic cognition arising from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of a real object (*bhūtārtha*) to possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
because it has the nature of memory (*smṛti*).
For cultivation is that which follows after a real object has been determined by a valid means of knowledge.
That is merely a continuous stream of memory;

even the knowledge produced by its excellence is simply a specific kind of memory and thus not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is it perception (*pratyakṣa*). Enough with this excessive detail.
The restatement and refutation of the author of the *Vṛtti*’s view:

As for what some consider to be the definition of perception— namely, "the arising of cognition in a person when there is contact between the sense organs and that [object] is true perception" (NS 1.1.4)—
that too is not a valid definition because it lacks pervasiveness (*avyāpaka*).
Even the cognition arising from a mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, when directed toward one's own self, is accepted as being perceptual (*pratyakṣa*);
and since all cognitions are intended to be perceptual with respect to their own nature, why is it said [in the definition]: "when there is contact with that"?
It is said: those who assert that even cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell are perception are refuted.
For among objects of knowledge in the world, only that [cognition] is called "perception" whose object is the thing itself.
Therefore, that cognition which arises for a person when there is contact with the sense-faculties [is perception].
However, the cognition of silver that arises when the eye is in contact with mother-of-pearl is not of this kind.
Consequently, the cognition of silver is not perception.
For the cognition of silver has silver as its object,
yet the sense organ is not in contact with the silver, because the silver is not present there.
Therefore, it must be explained that this sūtra is intended to demonstrate that the cognition of silver is not perception, but rather memory.
The definition of perception according to the opinion of the Guru [Dharmottara]:
Now he states his own intended definition of perception: "Perception is immediate cognition" (*sākṣātpratītiḥ pratyakṣam*).
But would it not follow that even memory, which arises at the culmination of the intensity of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), is perception, since it possesses immediacy? No.
Because this is the section concerning the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
since direct experience (*anubhūti*) is the means of valid cognition, and perception (*pratyakṣa*) is a specific type of that, memory (*smṛti*) does not incur the status of being perception.
He states the object of perception: "It [perception] exists with respect to the object of knowledge, the knower, and the means of knowledge.

He provides the classification therein: "Arising from the contact of the senses with objects" refers to that perceptual cognition arising from the conjunction of the senses with substances, universals, and qualities—[that is,] through the contact of the senses with the objects of knowledge, or through inherence in what is conjoined with them.
And it arises through inherence.
What, then, are the sense organs? They are the external ones: the olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, and auditory.
And there is the internal mind.
But what is the means of valid cognition for their existence and their distinction?
It is said: first of all, the cognition of an object is observed to be occasional;
its self (ātman) is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), and an effect is not produced without a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa).
And that non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) must be in close proximity to the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).
This proximity is observed to be of two kinds: inherence in the same effect (kāryasamavāya) and inherence in the same cause (tatkāraṇasamavāya).
For instance, the conjunction with fire (agnisaṃyoga), being an inherent cause residing in the substance being cooked, produces fragrance and other qualities in that very same substance.
The forms of the threads, inhering in the threads which constitute the cause of the cloth, are the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of the form of the cloth.

In that regard, since the self is eternal, there can be no non-inherent cause inherent in its own cause; therefore, another quality inherent in the self itself must be accepted as the non-inherent cause.
In this context, it has been established that for a specific quality (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*) inherent in an eternal substance, conjunction with another substance alone functions as the non-inherent cause.

In the case of earth-atoms (*pārthivaparamāṇu*), color and other qualities are observed to arise by depending solely upon conjunction with fire as their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Therefore, the property called "cognition" (*bodha*) belonging to the self (*ātman*) must also depend solely upon conjunction with another substance as its non-inherent cause.

Since there is no evidence for the existence of another substance that could serve as the substratum for that [conjunction], it is determined that the self is a substance that is not composed of further substances (*adravyadravya*). Furthermore, substances that are not composed of further substances are of two kinds: those that are infinitely large (*paramamahat*), such as space (*ākāśa*), and those that are atomic (*paramāṇu*).
In that case, if one were to admit a distinct substance possessing supreme magnitude, conjunction itself would be untenable,
because of the absence of a cause for conjunction.
For whatever conjunction is directly perceived, [it requires a cause].
It is produced by the action of one, produced by the actions of both,
or produced by conjunction.
Since conjunction is understood through that fixed causality,
it is determined that in the absence of that [cause], conjunction itself does not exist;
moreover, a direct conjunction between two all-pervading [substances] does not occur.
Since it cannot be inferred [as being large], by the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya), its atomicity alone is accepted.
And since it is atomic, the arising of conjunction through the power of its own action is not untenable.
Furthermore, in the production of that action, the cause is precisely the conjunction of the self with something possessing effort.
It is like the action of the body;
and in the absence of effort, it has as its cause the conjunction of the self with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), like the horizontal movement of air.
As it has been said: "The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of air, and the initial action of atoms and of the mind are caused by the unseen force."
That which is the cause of the experience of cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort— that distinct substance designated by the term "manas" (mind)—
must be understood as an independent cause, assisted in all instances of memory by the cooperative factor of the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by previous perceptions.
By this, that which they say— namely, "That consciousness which has just passed away from among the six is the mind" (Abhidharmakośa,
Chapter 1, Verse 17)—
is also refuted.

Because it is observed that the conjunction with another substance serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the production of specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*) residing in eternal substances;

and because light, though possessing color, is seen to be a causal factor in the perception of color, one must conclude that the sense organ, like [light] which possesses color, is the causal factor for the perception of color.
Likewise, [the olfactory organ], like that which possesses odor, is the causal factor in the perception of odor.
Likewise— the sense organ is the cause for the apprehension of touch,
just as [the tongue] is the cause for the apprehension of taste;
it is the cause for the apprehension of sound, just as [the ear] is the cause for the apprehension of sound.
Thus it should be understood:
therefore, the olfactory organ, being earthy and possessing fragrance, is the cause for perceiving odors;
and the gustatory organ, belonging to water and possessing taste, is the instrumental cause for the experience of tastes.
The visual organ, being composed of fire, possesses form and is the cause of the perception of form.

The tactile organ, being composed of air, possesses touch and is the cause of the apprehension of touch. Space, possessing the quality of sound, is the auditory organ and the cause of the apprehension of sound.

Even for an object that has entered into a connection with a sense organ, it is not perceived by one whose mind is attached to another object; therefore, the dependence of the sense organs upon the conjunction with the mind is established.

Consequently, in the apprehension of internal objects such as pleasure and the like, two types of contact are the cause: the contact known as the conjunction of the self and the mind, and the contact between the mind and pleasure (or the like), which is characterized as inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).
Furthermore, in the apprehension of external objects such as color and so forth, there are four types of contact as causes: contact between the self and the mind,
contact between the mind and the sense organ,
contact between the substance and the sense organ, and contact between the color-form and the sense organ.
He states the classification of the objects of cognition (*prameya*): “It [the perception] occurs with respect to substance, genus, and quality.
This cognition, arising from contact with the sense organs, occurs with respect to substance, genus, and quality.
A substance possessing touch and magnitude is an earthy one.
The watery,
the fiery,
and the airy.
The sensory [perception] is of four kinds;
it is the cause for the arising of such substances, and the proof regarding that has been determined in the *Jātinirṇaya*.
The existence of genus (*jāti*) has also been explained in the very determination of genus itself.

As for quality (*guṇa*): color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, and effort are perceptible by the senses;
furthermore, even when a substance is not perceived, there is sometimes the perception of its color and other qualities.
"Even when color and so forth are not apprehended, there is the [apprehension] of the substance"— thus,
there is no fixed rule regarding the apprehension of substances and qualities.
Furthermore, this cognition of substances and so forth is of two kinds.
“Perceptual cognition is held to be both conceptual and non-conceptual.
[The author] analyzes this: “The first has a qualified object; the other has its own nature as its object.”
Thus,
first of all, the apprehension of the mere intrinsic nature (svarūpa) is possible in the case of substances, universals, and qualities;
and that is established by one's own experience.

For one whose mind is concentrated and devoid of pursuit of other objects perceives directly the object connected with the sense faculty; thus, self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here.
This is the investigation of non-conceptual [perception].
Its object is not merely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Because the appearance of the forms of genus and so forth is vivid,
nor is the universal alone the object,
since the apprehension of particularity is established by experience.

187. As for what is stated in [Brahmasiddhi], beginning with “In some cases, something [is perceived] when its form has been apprehended,” that refers to the object of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and not to the object of the difference between real entities (*vastubheda*).
For it is only after the cognition of the distinction between two entities that their mutual non-existence is determined.
Having cognized a jar as having the form of a jar and a cloth as having the form of a cloth, one realizes their mutual non-existence by thinking, "This is not that."
Furthermore, since the cognition of a jar and the like does not depend upon the apprehension of another entity, its apprehension is not untenable even when that other entity is not perceived.
Therefore, it is first logically established that perception apprehends two entities: the universal and the particular.
However, because it is devoid of any investigation into other entities, it is not perceived as both a universal and a particular;
for that which is inclusive is called a universal, while exclusion is the particular.
Furthermore, without the consideration of another entity, it is not possible to comprehend both the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the exclusion (*vyatireka*);
yet, even while not comprehending those two, one is indeed able to comprehend their own nature.

Non-conceptual [perception] has as its object neither the universal nor the particular. Conceptual determination follows it; however, that conceptual [cognition], occurring subsequent to it, apprehends those very same objects by way of their nature as universals and particulars.
But surely, the sense organ is not capable of apprehending another object;
and since perception arises from the capacity of the sense organ,
how can the object of perception consist of both the universal and the particular?
It is said: This would indeed be so if the sense organs themselves were conscious, or if they were cognitions.

But the Self is one, the experiencer of all that is to be experienced; by virtue of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it connects one thing with another and is indeed capable of apprehending an object through a sense organ as consisting of both the universal and the particular.
Likewise, even by means of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), which perceives the two entities—the universal and the particular—their difference cannot be grasped.
For the cognition of difference does not arise from the mere difference of entities;
rather, the apprehension of another property (*dharmāntara*) is also a cooperative factor in the cognition of difference.

Therefore, for one who does not apprehend positive concomitance (*anugati*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) as distinct properties, there was no cognition of difference even though a difference between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) existed.
And at a later time, by means of the recollection of another object, those two are apprehended and their difference is determined;

since the determination of the relationship between qualifier and qualified occurs only when there is difference, there is no cognition of a qualified entity during the stage of indeterminate perception.
In the state of conceptualization (*savikalpaka*), however, one perceives the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
Even when a quality is perceived, indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) does not delimit the substance as being qualified,
because the difference between the substance and the quality has not yet been apprehended.
For it is through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the difference between qualities (*guṇa*) and universals (*jāti*) from substance (*dravya*) is understood.
Since such coordination of positive and negative concomitance does not exist in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*),
there is no apprehension of difference by means of it.
And since that [object], when its difference is not grasped, cannot be apprehended as qualified, the cognition of a qualified object is necessarily conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
Even in the conceptualization of a name, it is only the denotability by a word, when being remembered, that serves as the qualifier.
The conceptualization of an action (*karma-kalpanā*) is likewise to be explained in this same way.
Even when a qualifier is presented by another cognition, a qualified cognition certainly arises.

Since the self is the knower (*pramātṛ*), and because determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) follows upon indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) should be understood—despite its grasping what has already been grasped—by way of the principle of the continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika-nyāya*).
Furthermore, it is indeed possible for determinate cognition to grasp what was not previously grasped, even apart from the relation between the qualified and the qualifier.
Furthermore, its having external objects as its domain was established in the *Jātinirṇaya*;
nor is this cognition non-sensory,
because its activity is dependent upon the sense organs.
For this conceptual cognition (savikalpakapratyaya) is indeed the manifestation of an object as directly perceived;
such a thing does not exist without the operation of the sense organs.
[This is] the determination by means of the threefold division.

Now, in order to explain perception (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to both the object of cognition (*miti*) and the cognizer (*mātṛ*), he says: "Valid cognition (*pramā*) arising from the causes of all cognitions is accepted as perception (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to both the object and the cognizer, due to the commonality of being a direct agent."
Thus:
whatever cognition of an object takes the form of apprehension or recollection, in that, the self shines forth directly.
For objects do not appear when their own nature, which manifests as the appearance of those objects, does not itself manifest.
Indeed, every cognition arises in this way: "I know this"; there is no cognition whatsoever that occurs merely as "it knows."
And at that time, since there would be no distinction between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another,
a restriction based on being the object of a different cognition is not possible;
for it is only when two things are objects of a single cognition that the rule of simultaneous apprehension is logical.
Therefore, by means of all causes of knowledge, a cognition characterized by direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) arises with respect to the self.
The determination of its status as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is made in relation to its object.
[Objection: If that is so, would it not follow that everything is perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
If it refers to the measure itself,
that is indeed accepted.
If it refers to the object of cognition, it is not so.
Because there is no rule that the object of cognition (*prameya*) must be directly perceived (*aparokṣa*) in all cases—
since in memory, inference, and so forth, the object of cognition is not directly perceived—
it should be understood that the designation of these as distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is made solely with respect to their objects.
Furthermore, all cognitions manifest themselves as direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, it is indeed logical that they possess both the nature of direct perception and the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to their own selves.

An examination of the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of knowledge. What is the distinction regarding the cognition of the object (*meyam*), the subject (*mātṛ*), and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? It is said: with respect to the object and the subject, the cognition is distinct and possesses the character of direct perception (*sākṣātkāravat*).
In the case of valid cognition (*miti*), however, it is non-distinct [from its object];
for in such instances as "I perceive this" or "I remember this," only a triad appears.
This consciousness is of the nature of appearing as the measure alone;
however, no other consciousness shines within it,
nor does it fail to shine itself.
If that [consciousness] were not manifest, it would follow that everything is unmanifest.
Furthermore, let the objects of cognition (*meyāni*) have a non-luminous nature, and let the cognizer (*mātā*) depend upon luminosity.
Light, however, because its very nature is luminosity, does not depend on anything else;
for when one is awake, both the objects of cognition and the cognizer shine forth,
whereas in deep sleep, even that duality does not manifest.
And at that time, it is not the case that those two do not exist at all,
because they are recognized upon awakening;
for if they were of the nature of mere light, those two would be manifest even during the state of deep sleep.
Therefore, both of those [the object and the subject] are admitted to be non-luminous by nature;
however, the very existence of luminosity itself is not accepted if it were not manifesting.
Consequently, the manifestation of the object and the subject occurs only through the principle of self-luminosity.
Furthermore, when something is established by its own nature alone, dependence on another is not logical;
for it is not the case that the self-luminosity of both the objects of cognition and the cognizer is untenable.
It is logical that those two depend on something else;
however, since there is no inconsistency whatsoever regarding the act of cognition itself, cognition is self-luminous.
This is the prima facie argument according to the Sautrāntika school.
Regarding this, they say: If cognition is accepted as self-luminous, then, since it is impossible for that which is formless to be luminous, a form must necessarily be admitted.
And this form appears as one.
Therefore, it is logical that manifestation itself possesses that form.
Furthermore, if manifestation were devoid of form, the systematic distinction between one action and another would not be possible;
for there would be no distinction in that manifestation with respect to all objects.
But if [cognition] possesses the form of the object, then the determination of each respective object is logical, in that "this is the form of that [object].
As they say: "For it is not tenable that the cognition of an object occurs merely by the existence of consciousness itself."
Because that [cognition] would lack distinction everywhere due to the consequence of non-distinction,
it must enter into similarity with the object and thus bring about the apprehension of that which is similar to it;
therefore, it is logical that the similarity to the object alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the validity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in their being determinative;
and it is the conformity with the object (*arthasārūpya*) that is the cause of determination,
not the eye and so forth.
Because that [object] is common to many subjects;
furthermore, the simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha*) of the cognition and the cognized object is invariably observed,
for there is never an apprehension of the cognized object apart from the cognition.
Nor is there [simultaneous perception] of consciousness devoid of an object of cognition.
Furthermore, regarding those entities that appear as mutually distinct, there is no rule of their simultaneous perception.
A jar and a cloth are not necessarily perceived together;
therefore, since non-necessity pervades difference, necessity—by being excluded from that [difference]—remains only in non-difference and thus establishes non-difference.
As it has been said: "Because of the necessity of simultaneous perception, there is no difference between the blue and its cognition."
By this very principle, the non-difference between the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) characterized by the form "I" and cognition (*vitti*) is to be established.

How, then, do cognitions possessing the forms of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) appear as mutually distinct? Regarding this, they say: "And the distinction is seen through erroneous cognitions, just as the duality [of the moon] is seen in the non-dual moon."
Thus it is said in the *Prakaraṇavārttika*, chapter 3, verse 389, and likewise elsewhere: “This internal division and this external portion [of cognition]—
this appearance as distinct within the non-dual cognition is indeed a cognitive distortion (*upaplava*).”
Thus, according to *Pravāhaparīkṣā* verse 212:
"In the delusion of difference, the cause is precisely the beginningless latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference."
This must be investigated: does this cognition, which possesses a specific form, arise from an external object, or rather from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
As it has been said: "If cognition possesses that form, then that [cognition] exists as qualified by that form;
it must then be subjected to this investigation: does it [arise] from an external object or from something else?"
Thus, in the *Prakaraṇaviniścaya* (Treatise on the Ascertainment of Topics), verse 334,
it is said:
"In that regard, the Sautrāntikas maintain that it is not tenable for a specific mental aspect (*ākāra*) to arise from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) alone."
Because it is impossible for there to be a fixed restriction of place and time,
even after the cognition of a jar, the cognition of a cloth arises;
and where a jar exists in an external location at a certain time, [the cognition of it occurs].

In that case, if the mere cognition of a jar were the cause for the arising of the cognition of a cloth, then whenever and wherever a cloth is absent, the cognition of a cloth would still occur there at that time.
But this is not the case;
therefore, there exists an object distinct from the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), namely the form of the cognition which is the cause of its attainment.
Furthermore, just as in the case of the cognition of water in a mirage, no purposeful action (arthakriyā) is possible for one who proceeds toward it seeking water.
Likewise, even in the case of a correct cognition of water, [such a distinction] would not exist;

for when there is no difference in being devoid of an object, it is not possible to make a distinction such as "this is a correct cognition of water" and "this is not. Therefore, it is appropriate to accept an external object as well.
The refutation of the Sautrāntika position according to the view of the Vijñānavādins:
Others consider that [position] to be erroneous.
For instance—it is not at all directly perceived anywhere that an object possesses the capacity to impart a specific form [to cognition].
But that must indeed be postulated.
And it is better to postulate that very thing as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) when it is observed.
Let the difference among the cognitions that constitute the effects be caused by the difference among their immediately preceding conditions.
Therefore, the establishment of specific restriction is that a particular cognition is the cause of a particular [effect] for a particular [person], in a particular place, at a particular time.

Furthermore, the Vijñānavādin considers even causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be of the very nature of cognition. Consequently, only a certain cognition of water is capable of producing causal efficiency.
Furthermore, there is the establishment of specific determination even in the case of "it is not so.

Moreover, one must necessarily admit the efficacy of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the arising of a cognition with a distinct form in the absence of an external object;
otherwise, there would be no specific determination regarding the appearance of forms in dreams and the like.
Nor is it the case that only those [causes] existing in another place or at another time possess efficacy there,
because that which is non-existent lacks the capacity for efficacy.
(238) If it is argued that the restriction regarding the appearance of a form therein arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by experience, [we reply:]...
Let it be so for now;

however, even that experience [of the object] may then arise here simply from the latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by another experience. Why, then, accept this [external] object through such a line of reasoning?
Furthermore, regarding the statement "a formation [arises] from a formation":
consciousness proceeds solely preceded by experience through the relationship of cause and effect;
thus, from that cognition which has the form of the experience of an object, another consciousness is produced.
That has a specific nature;
and whatever else follows from that,
that too is consciousness with a specific nature alone.
The very specific nature of consciousness itself is designated by such terms as "cultivation" (bhāvanā), "latent impression" (vāsanā), and "formative force" (saṃskāra).

Furthermore, the distinction between valid and invalid cognition is logically established: cognition that is capable of correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is valid, while the other is not.
Therefore, let cognitions possess specific forms and flow as an beginningless continuum through the relationship of cause and effect.
"There is no such thing as an object that exists apart from that [consciousness].
This is the refutation of the Vijñānavāda position.

To this, it is replied: First, as for what was stated—that for the sake of establishing that cognition possesses a form (sākāratva), the determination of specific objects (pratikarmavyavasthā) cannot be established without similarity to the object (arthasārūpya).
That is incorrect;
for the proponent of cognition with forms (sākāra-vijñānavādin) has not experienced the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of any object whatsoever,
because all cognitions function exclusively as the form of the cognition itself.
Furthermore, for one whose own nature (*svarūpa*) has not even been determined, there can be no conceptualization of similarity with anything else.
Nor can an object, when established by virtue of the arising of a form in cognition, be conceptually constructed as being similar [to that cognition].
Even from that which is dissimilar in form, the occurrence of the aspect found in the effect is possible;
for even when no distinction is perceived in the state of a sprout from a seed dyed with lac, the production of a red effect is observed.
Indeed, it is not the case that the cognition must arise with the same form [as its cause].
Regarding the claim that "the object possessing that very form is the cause for the arising of cognition," no proof whatsoever can be advanced here.
Furthermore, cognition arises with a gross form; it is a consciousness characterized by a common form.
If the object is its unique, specific form, then what constitutes "similarity" (sārūpya)? Furthermore,
if [the object] were cognizable merely by virtue of such similarity, the established distinction between the cognized and the cognizer would not be tenable.

Because it is impossible for cognitions belonging to different mental continua— which have the same object— to stand in the relationship of the perceived and the perceiver. Furthermore, if that which produces [a cognition] and imparts its own form is the perceived, then even so, each preceding cognition in a continuous stream would be the perceived object of each succeeding cognition.
Now, suppose it is argued that what is cognized is that which imparts a specific form [to consciousness];
even so, it follows that only each preceding cognition is what is cognized.
For it has been stated that each preceding cognition is the cause for the arising of a specific form.
Moreover, even if consciousness is formless (*nirākāra*), the determination of [cognition] according to each respective object is not untenable;
for consciousness is a specific attribute of the person that is conducive to the engagement in specific linguistic conventions bound to the object,
and it is self-luminous.
That which manifests as being conducive to linguistic and practical activity connected with a particular object is established as the cognition of that object;
furthermore, the rule of simultaneous apprehension is compatible even with difference.
For that which is the cognition of blue is itself the apprehension of the blue.
How could the blue be apprehended without the apprehension of the blue?
Furthermore, this leads to the following undesirable consequence:
that something would be perceived even without perception.
For it is not maintained that any entity whatsoever is perceived without perception.
For perception does not arise from perception alone.
Furthermore, the distinction between the perceiver and the perceived is pervaded by the rule of non-simultaneous perception;
therefore, that rule, when it is excluded [from the case of simultaneous perception], remains only in non-distinction, and being thus pervaded, it leads to the inference of that [non-distinction].
However, even if there is a difference between the apprehender and the apprehended, a necessary rule [of their simultaneous perception] is possible.
Therefore, although they are distinct, the observed necessity of their simultaneous apprehension is not capable of proving their non-difference.
Furthermore, the necessity of simultaneous apprehension exists even when there is a difference between consciousness and its object.
Furthermore, because that [object] would also result in being of the nature of cognition, the unity of cognition would be lost;
consequently, it follows that the necessity of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) pertains only to difference.
Moreover, even for one who asserts the non-difference of cognition from the object of cognition—
Even he does not disregard the appearance of the object of cognition;
for if that were the case, how could inference arise?
Indeed, inference cannot come into being through a reversal of perception.
Furthermore, even the inference of non-difference regarding flames and the like does not displace cognition from its own object;
rather, it demonstrates that there are two cognitions— consisting of perception and recollection— both directed toward a fixed object, such as "this is that very same flame."
In this case, however, the perception of difference must itself be set aside by that which is to be cognized;
therefore, an inference does not arise in contradiction with it.
"And difference is seen by erroneous cognitions, just as [duality] is seen in the non-dual moon."
And this [assertion] is untenable;
for no actual division is perceived there, but rather, with respect to a single moon, two cognitions arise due to the different modes of the visual faculty.

It has been stated in various places that, although the moon is not actually divided, deluded people engage in a dualistic linguistic convention regarding it as two distinct objects due to the difference in the functioning of their respective sense organs.
Furthermore, as for this which was said— that the form of blue and so forth exists within consciousness, which is admitted to be self-luminous— [it is refuted as follows:]...
That too is incorrect;
for it is impossible for a form (ākāra) appearing as non-different from consciousness to be of the nature of consciousness.
If it is asked, "How can consciousness be manifest if it is formless?"
What is meant by "formless" (*nirākāra*)?
If it means "devoid of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*),
that is incorrect, because consciousness is admitted to have consciousness as its intrinsic nature.
Now, if it is argued that [consciousness] has the form of blue and so forth,

what royal decree is there that it must be manifested only by the form of blue and so forth, and not by anything else? For when manifestation occurs, whatever is perceived in whatever manner, that [is how it is].
It is therefore logical to accept that it is of such a nature.
As for what was said— that in a dream the form of cognition appears—
that too is incorrect.
Even in that case, because consciousness appears as if external,
it does not follow that it lacks an external object;
