for, by virtue of the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by previous experiences, its object is indeed the thing previously experienced.
How, then, is the state of having been previously experienced not recollected, or how is there the determination that something is being presently experienced? It is said in reply:
This memory is held to have the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as its cause; and the awakening of the latent impression is dependent upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*),
because that [unseen force] is the cause of pleasure and pain.
Because pleasure and pain are experienced even in a dream, that unseen force (adṛṣṭa) awakens the latent impression (saṃskāra) only to that extent, namely,
only as far as the pleasure or pain actually arises.
Furthermore, pleasure and pain do not arise from the recollection of a portion of what was previously experienced;
nor is there an awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) therein,
nor even recollection (*smṛti*).
For this very reason, since there is no determination of the apprehended parts, nothing remains but mere experience; thus, even the determination of experience is established.
As for what they [the opponents] say—that because an insentient thing cannot be manifest, the form must be of the nature of light itself—that too is not tenable.
What is meant by "insentient" (*jaḍa*)?

If you say it means "having a nature that is non-luminous," no; for that very thing which is non-luminous and distinct from luminosity is established as "this is its illumination" precisely through luminosity itself.

Furthermore, regarding the cognition of a variegated cloth (*citrapaṭa*), since it is contradictory for multiple forms to have the nature of a single manifestation, their very unreality must be admitted.
If unity is not tenable among the objects appearing as variegated,
how indeed can that cognition itself be a single [entity] manifesting as variegated?
Having raised this objection, it was said: "This is the reality established by the force of facts, as the wise declare:
in whatever way objects are reflected upon, in that very way they are analyzed. (Pramāṇavārttika, Chapter 2, Verse 208)
[Pravāraṇāvādadvitīyapariccheda, verse 205].
Just as forms are investigated, so too are they analyzed as being untenable—they become empty; that is to say, they become non-existent.
Furthermore, since those forms of yours are non-existent and do not possess the nature of manifestation,
how can they manifest? Likewise, how could the absolute non-existence of the distinction between the grasped, the grasper, and consciousness— which does not enter into manifestation— ever manifest?

Likewise, the various modes of denying external objects that arise from the investigation of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) have for the most part already been formulated and refuted in the *Jātinirṇaya*;
therefore, they are not introduced here.

However, those who seek to establish the emptiness of external objects by means of the reason "because they are cognitions," using waking cognitions as the subject and dream cognitions as the example, [are addressed next].
Their thesis contradicts the universal perception of external objects.

Furthermore, since even the dream-cognition adduced as an example is supported by the existence of external apprehended objects, the fault of the reason being contradictory (*viruddhatva*) and the deficiency of the example lacking the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*) must be pointed out.
Therefore, it is established that even though consciousness is self-luminous (*svayamprakāśa*), there is no denial of external objects of apprehension.

[This concludes] the removal of doubts regarding the self-luminosity of consciousness. As for those who say: "Just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself by itself," [so too consciousness cannot know itself].
In this same way, even cognition cannot arise by itself through its own nature.
[Commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad] Thus it is said.
In that regard, if it is argued that the status of being both object and agent is untenable,
then nothing is lost.
For we do not accept the relationship of object and agent [in this case].
If, however, the self-luminosity of that which has the nature of manifesting an object is denied,
then there is a contradiction with experience.
Furthermore, how could those who, by the force of common experience, accept that a single self possesses the status of both agent and object, deny consciousness itself?
Moreover, it is held that cognition is an object of inference.
In that inference, the mere existence of the object is not the logical mark (*liṅga*),
because there is no rule of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between it and that [inference]. If, on the other hand, it is said to be the cognition of the object, [then...]
Even that [cognition] is not a logical mark (liṅga) by virtue of its mere arising;
for when it is not manifest, there is no distinction between what has arisen and what has not arisen.
Indeed, a logical mark that is not manifest does not lead one to infer the possessor of the mark (liṅgin).
Furthermore, the manifestation of the cognition of an object does not depend on another cognition,
nor is there comprehension [of that cognition] through another cognition;
for if there were comprehension through another cognition, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.
Therefore, the cognition of an object must be admitted to be self-luminous.
By this, those who claim that the existence of cognition is established by another cognition— just as pleasure and so forth are perceived through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*)—
are also refuted.
It has already been stated that since self-luminosity is a logical possibility, the postulation of dependence on another is untenable.
What, then, is it that is inferred? It is cognition (*jñāna*).
But surely that is not perceived as distinct from consciousness (*saṃvit*), which is self-luminous?
True; for this very reason it is inferred. But we do not know what that is.
Let your long-lived self be satisfied by understanding that it is the contact between the self and the mind, which is the cause for the arising of consciousness.

He explains the absence of a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as follows: "If consciousness itself is the means of valid cognition, then the external result consists of rejection, acquisition, and so forth;
however, for knowledge, that very [consciousness] is the result when it is employed in practical activity."

Thus, when the derivation of the word *pramāṇa* as a state (*bhāvasādhana*)— meaning that valid cognition (*pramiti*) is the instrument of knowledge— is adopted, then consciousness alone (*saṃvid*) is the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And because that [cognition] has a nature conducive to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), its results are avoidance, acquisition, and indifference. When the word *pramāṇa* is derived in the sense of an instrument— meaning "that by which something is correctly cognized"— if the self-cognition (*jñāna*) arising from the contact between the self and the mind is the means of valid cognition, then the resulting consciousness itself, being serviceable for external transaction, is the result.

280. “The instrument (karaṇa) is relative; it may be the mind, or the sense faculty itself, or the contact between that [faculty] and its object. If this [contact] is the means of knowledge, then the former [the faculty] is the result.”
Thus [it is said].

However, since the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and since the suffix *-tama* denotes excellence, and since excellence is relative to something external, the sense organ itself—dependent on light and so forth—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
its contact with the object is [the instrumental cause].
Or else, the contact of that [self] with the mind is the means of valid cognition;
even then, consciousness alone is the result,
because the instruments of proof are directed toward that [consciousness].

Furthermore, those proponents who assert that the result is non-different from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are likewise to be disregarded, precisely because there is no identity between cause and effect.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Investigation of Direct Perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*), within the *Prakaraṇapāñcikā* composed by the Great Professor Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra.
